_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for South Korea (Republic of Korea) covering ancient Gojoseon, Three Kingdoms (Goguryeo/Baekje/Silla), Unified Silla, Goryeo, Joseon Dynasty, Japanese colonization 1910-1945, post-WWII US occupation zone, Korean War 1950-1953 (ceasefire/DMZ), authoritarian rule (Rhee, Park Chung-hee, Chun Doo-hwan), democratization 1987, IMF crisis 1997, Hallyu (Korean Wave), 'Miracle on Han River', chaebols, and K-pop global dominance.

religion.note: Rapid Christianization (was 2% in 1950); megachurches (Yoido Full Gospel, world's largest); shamanic mudang traditions persist; Confucian social values (filial piety, hierarchy); secularization increasing; Buddhist temples (Bulguksa, Haeinsa)

ethnic_groups.name: Korean
ethnic_groups.notes: Ethnically homogeneous; strong ethnic nationalism; 'Han' identity (distinct from Chinese Han); single ethnicity narrative (historically inaccurate but politically enforced); Seoul-centric; Jeolla/Gyeongsang regional rivalries

ethnic_groups.name: Chinese (Korean-Chinese/Hwagyo)
ethnic_groups.notes: Mostly ethnic Koreans from China (joseonjok/Chaoxianzu); Incheon Chinatown; some discrimination

ethnic_groups.name: Other (Southeast Asian, South Asian, Western)
ethnic_groups.notes: Migrant workers; Filipino/Vietnamese/Thai brides (rural men); 'multicultural families'; growing but face discrimination; small refugee population

independence.from: Declared independence from Japanese colonial rule (1945 liberation); separate from North Korea

country_profile.notes_unique: 'Miracle on Han River' (1960s-90s economic boom); Korean War (1950-53, ~3M dead, technically ongoing - armistice only); DMZ world's most militarized border; chaebols (Samsung, Hyundai, LG); K-pop (BTS, Blackpink); K-drama (Squid Game, Parasite Oscar 2020); world's lowest birth rate (0.72 in 2023); mandatory military service (18-21 months); han-geul alphabet (Sejong, 1443); kimchi; PC bang (gaming cafes); fastest internet globally; Gwangju Uprising 1980; Sewol ferry disaster 2014

current_leader.name: Yoon Suk Yeol
current_leader.title: President
current_leader.notes: People Power Party (conservative); former prosecutor; hard line on North Korea; pro-US/Japan; wife Kim Keon Hee controversies; unpopular; narrow election win over Lee Jae-myung

former_leaders.name: Moon Jae-in
former_leaders.notes: Democratic Party (liberal); human rights lawyer; North Korea engagement (summits with Kim Jong Un 2018-19); 'Sunshine Policy' revival; popular; prosecuted Park/Lee predecessors

former_leaders.name: Park Geun-hye
former_leaders.notes: First female president; daughter of dictator Park Chung-hee; impeached (Choi Soon-sil corruption scandal); 24-year prison sentence (later pardoned 2021); candle protests 2016-17

former_leaders.name: Lee Myung-bak
former_leaders.notes: Conservative; former Hyundai CEO/Seoul mayor; 'Four River Project'; later convicted of corruption (15 years, pardoned by Yoon 2022); North Korea tensions (Cheonan sinking, Yeonpyeong shelling)

former_leaders.name: Roh Moo-hyun
former_leaders.notes: Liberal; human rights lawyer; progressive; North Korea engagement; corruption investigations (family); suicide 2009 (jumped off cliff)

former_leaders.name: Kim Dae-jung
former_leaders.notes: 'Sunshine Policy' (North Korea engagement); 2000 inter-Korean summit (Nobel Peace Prize); IMF crisis recovery; democracy icon; survived assassination attempts under military rule; died 2009

former_leaders.name: Kim Young-sam
former_leaders.notes: First civilian president in 32 years; anti-corruption; imprisoned Chun/Roh (coup leaders); IMF crisis 1997 (humiliation)

former_leaders.name: Roh Tae-woo
former_leaders.notes: General; 1987 democratization concessions; Seoul Olympics 1988; later imprisoned (coup/corruption); pardoned

former_leaders.name: Chun Doo-hwan
former_leaders.notes: General; 1979 coup; Gwangju Massacre 1980 (~200+ killed); authoritarian; economic growth; 1988 Olympics preparations; later imprisoned (coup/corruption); died 2021

former_leaders.name: Park Chung-hee
former_leaders.notes: General; 1961 coup; dictator; economic miracle architect; chaebols; Yushin Constitution 1972 (absolute power); assassinated by KCIA director Kim Jae-gyu (dinner); father of Park Geun-hye

former_leaders.name: Syngman Rhee
former_leaders.notes: First president; Princeton PhD; authoritarian; Korean War; rigged election 1960 sparked April Revolution; resigned, exiled to Hawaii; died 1965

910.name: Prehistoric Korea and Gojoseon
910.description: The earliest inhabitants of the Korean Peninsula, the Jeulmun and Mumun pottery periods, the bronze culture of the dolmen builders, and the legendary kingdom of Gojoseon.

sub_clusters.name: Neolithic and Bronze Age Korea
sub_clusters.description: The Jeulmun comb-pattern pottery, Mumun period agriculture and megalithic dolmens (Korea has the world's largest concentration), bronze daggers and mirrors, and the development of chiefdom societies.
key_events: Korean Peninsula contains over 40% of the world's dolmens — the largest concentration on Earth

sub_clusters.name: Samhan Confederacies
sub_clusters.description: The Mahan, Jinhan, and Byeonhan confederacies of southern Korea, iron production and trade with Japan and China, and the proto-state formations that would evolve into Baekje, Silla, and Gaya.

910.name: Three Kingdoms of Korea
910.description: The golden age of the Three Kingdoms — Goguryeo, Baekje, and Silla — along with the Gaya confederacy, their rivalry, cultural brilliance, and Silla's eventual unification of the peninsula.

sub_clusters.name: Baekje Kingdom
sub_clusters.description: The cultured southwestern kingdom of Baekje, its Buddhist art and architecture, the crucial transmission of Chinese culture to Japan, and its destruction by the Tang-Silla alliance.
key_events: Baekje transmits Buddhism, Chinese writing, and advanced culture to Japan (4th–6th centuries)

sub_clusters.name: Silla Kingdom and Gaya
sub_clusters.description: Silla's gradual rise from the southeast, the magnificent gold crowns and tombs of Gyeongju, the Gaya iron confederacy, Silla's alliance with Tang China, and the unification wars.
key_events: Silla's alliance with Tang China destroys Baekje (660) and Goguryeo (668) — peninsula unified

sub_clusters.name: Unified Silla
sub_clusters.description: The golden age of Unified Silla centered at Gyeongju, the magnificent Bulguksa Temple and Seokguram Grotto, the expulsion of Tang forces from Korea, and the eventual decline and fragmentation.
key_events: Bulguksa Temple and Seokguram Grotto constructed — masterpieces of Korean Buddhist art (751)
Silla expels Tang forces and secures control of the peninsula south of the Taedong River (676)

920.name: Goryeo Dynasty
920.description: The dynasty that gave Korea its Western name, renowned for celadon ceramics, the Tripitaka Koreana, the world's first metal movable type, and its struggle against Mongol domination.

sub_clusters.name: Goryeo Foundation and Golden Age
sub_clusters.description: Wang Geon's unification, the development of the civil service examination system, the exquisite celadon pottery, the invention of metal movable type printing, and Buddhist cultural flourishing.
key_events: World's first metal movable type used to print the Jikji — predating Gutenberg by 78 years (1377)

sub_clusters.name: Military Rule and Mongol Period
sub_clusters.description: The military coup of 1170, the slave rebellion of Manjŏk, the Mongol invasions and vassalage, the Ssangseong Commandery dispute, and General Yi Seong-gye's overthrow of Goryeo.
key_events: Goryeo becomes a Mongol vassal — royal family intermarries with Yuan dynasty (1270)

920.name: Joseon Dynasty
920.description: Korea's longest-lasting dynasty, the Neo-Confucian transformation of society, King Sejong's creation of Hangul, the Imjin War against Japan, and the hermit kingdom era.

sub_clusters.name: Early Joseon and King Sejong
sub_clusters.description: Yi Seong-gye's founding of the Joseon dynasty, the adoption of Neo-Confucianism as state ideology, and King Sejong the Great's creation of Hangul, the Korean alphabet — one of the most scientific writing systems ever devised.
key_events: King Sejong the Great promulgates Hangul — the Korean alphabet (1443–1446)

sub_clusters.name: Imjin War and Admiral Yi Sun-sin
sub_clusters.description: Toyotomi Hideyoshi's invasion of Korea, the devastating seven-year war, Admiral Yi Sun-sin's legendary naval victories with the turtle ships, Chinese intervention, and the war's enormous human cost.
key_events: Admiral Yi Sun-sin defeats the Japanese navy at the Battle of Myeongnyang with 13 ships against 133 (1597)

sub_clusters.name: Late Joseon and Hermit Kingdom
sub_clusters.description: The Manchu invasions, the Silhak (Practical Learning) reform movement, the Catholic persecutions, the Heungseon Daewongun's isolationist policies, and the opening of Korea by foreign powers.
key_events: Japan forces the Treaty of Ganghwa — opening Korea to foreign trade (1876)

930.name: Korean Empire and Japanese Colonization
930.description: The brief Korean Empire, Japan's annexation of Korea, the March 1st Movement, colonial modernization and exploitation, the comfort women tragedy, and the struggle for independence.

sub_clusters.name: Korean Empire and Annexation
sub_clusters.description: Emperor Gojong's declaration of the Korean Empire, the Russo-Japanese War fought on Korean soil, the Eulsa Treaty reducing Korea to a protectorate, and Japan's full annexation.
key_events: Japan formally annexes Korea — beginning 35 years of colonial rule (August 22, 1910)

sub_clusters.name: Colonial Resistance and Independence Movement
sub_clusters.description: The March 1st Movement of 1919, the Korean Provisional Government in Shanghai, cultural suppression and forced labor, the comfort women system, and liberation at war's end.
key_events: March 1st Movement — two million Koreans protest Japanese rule in nationwide demonstrations (1919)
Korean Provisional Government established in Shanghai (1919)

940.name: Division, Korean War, and First Republic
940.description: The American occupation south of the 38th parallel, the founding of the Republic of Korea under Syngman Rhee, the devastating Korean War, and the April Revolution.

sub_clusters.name: American Occupation and ROK Founding
sub_clusters.description: The US military government, the suppression of the Jeju Uprising, the UN-supervised elections, and the establishment of the Republic of Korea under President Syngman Rhee.
key_events: Republic of Korea proclaimed with Syngman Rhee as first president (August 15, 1948)
Jeju Uprising and massacre — up to 30,000 killed in anti-communist campaign (1948–1949)

sub_clusters.name: Korean War — Southern Perspective
sub_clusters.description: The North Korean invasion, the Busan Perimeter, MacArthur's Incheon landing, Chinese intervention, the stalemate, and the armistice that left Korea divided with over 3 million dead.
key_events: MacArthur's amphibious landing at Incheon — turns the tide of the war (September 15, 1950)

940.name: Park Chung-hee and Industrialization
940.description: Park Chung-hee's military coup, authoritarian developmentalism, the Miracle on the Han River transforming South Korea from one of the world's poorest countries to an industrial power, and his assassination.

sub_clusters.name: Military Coup and Economic Planning
sub_clusters.description: Park's seizure of power, the Five-Year Economic Plans, normalization with Japan, the dispatch of troops to Vietnam, the chaebol system, and the export-oriented industrialization strategy.
key_events: Park Chung-hee seizes power in a military coup (May 16, 1961)
Korea-Japan normalization treaty — controversial but provides crucial development capital (1965)

sub_clusters.name: Yushin Constitution and Heavy Industry
sub_clusters.description: The authoritarian Yushin Constitution, the Heavy and Chemical Industry drive, the Gyeongbu Expressway, the Saemaul Undong rural modernization movement, and Park's assassination by the KCIA director.
key_events: Park Chung-hee assassinated by KCIA Director Kim Jae-gyu (October 26, 1979)

950.name: Democratization Movement
950.description: The Gwangju Uprising, Chun Doo-hwan's authoritarian rule, the 1987 June Democracy Movement, the 1988 Seoul Olympics, and the transition to full civilian democracy.

sub_clusters.name: Gwangju Uprising and Fifth Republic
sub_clusters.description: The Gwangju Massacre where hundreds of civilians were killed by martial law troops, Chun Doo-hwan's authoritarian Fifth Republic, labor unrest, and the growing pro-democracy movement.
key_events: Gwangju Uprising — martial law troops kill hundreds of pro-democracy protesters (May 1980)

sub_clusters.name: June Democracy Movement and Olympics
sub_clusters.description: The June 29 Declaration conceding direct presidential elections, Roh Tae-woo's presidency, the landmark 1988 Seoul Olympics showcasing South Korea to the world, and the transition to civilian government.
key_events: June Democracy Movement forces democratic concessions (June 1987)
Seoul hosts the Olympic Games — South Korea's coming-out party to the world (1988)

950.name: Asian Financial Crisis and Sunshine Policy
950.description: Kim Young-sam's civilian government, the devastating 1997 Asian Financial Crisis and IMF bailout, Kim Dae-jung's Sunshine Policy toward North Korea, and the Korean Wave's emergence.

sub_clusters.name: IMF Crisis
sub_clusters.description: The Asian Financial Crisis devastating the Korean economy, the humiliating IMF bailout, citizens donating gold to pay national debt, chaebol restructuring, and the remarkably rapid recovery.
key_events: South Korea receives $58 billion IMF bailout — the 'IMF Crisis' reshapes the economy (1997)

sub_clusters.name: Sunshine Policy and Inter-Korean Summit
sub_clusters.description: President Kim Dae-jung's engagement with North Korea, the historic 2000 Inter-Korean Summit, the Nobel Peace Prize, the 2002 FIFA World Cup co-hosted with Japan, and the early Korean Wave.
key_events: First Inter-Korean Summit — Kim Dae-jung meets Kim Jong-il in Pyongyang (June 2000)
South Korea and Japan co-host the FIFA World Cup — South Korea reaches semifinals (2002)

960.name: Korean Wave and Contemporary South Korea
960.description: The global explosion of Hallyu (Korean Wave), K-pop and K-drama conquering world culture, the Sewol ferry disaster, the candlelight revolution impeaching President Park Geun-hye, and South Korea as a cultural superpower.

sub_clusters.name: Hallyu and Global Cultural Influence
sub_clusters.description: BTS and K-pop's global dominance, Parasite winning the Academy Award for Best Picture, Squid Game as Netflix's most-watched series, Samsung and Hyundai as global brands, and South Korea's soft power revolution.
key_events: PSY's 'Gangnam Style' becomes the first YouTube video to reach 1 billion views (2012)
Bong Joon-ho's Parasite wins Best Picture at the Academy Awards — first non-English language film (2020)

sub_clusters.name: Candlelight Revolution and Political Turbulence
sub_clusters.description: The massive candlelight protests leading to President Park Geun-hye's impeachment, the Moon Jae-in presidency, the inter-Korean summits of 2018, COVID-19 response, and political polarization.
key_events: Candlelight Revolution — millions protest; President Park Geun-hye impeached (2016–2017)
Inter-Korean summits and Singapore US-DPRK summit raise hopes for peace (2018)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
